title: A Lamb’s Ode to “Loverboy”
body:
A Lamb’s Ode to “Loverboy”

“Loverboy (Remix)” Mariah Carey, Glitter (2001)

I’m not sure why, but too many years elapsed before Mariah Carey would even acknowledge Glitter (2001). Considered a misfire by most outside of her fandom, mentions of “Loverboy” and Glitter were met with derision and jokes about her mental health. Granted, Glitter was an ambitious reimagining of Mariah’s life story-cum-A Star is Born at the intersection of 2001 Pop and 1983 Funk. For many critics, “ambitious” was considered an understatement: Carey’s vehicle crashed, both the box office and in critics’ hearts. For this lamb, who attempts to moonlight as a critic, I cannot help but make sense of the wreck, because context helps me to understand, and once I do, I get to enjoy.

The Glitter soundtrack’s poor commercial performance reflected a tepid reception to Mariah Carey at the time. What’s worse, Carey’s highly documented mental exhaustion, coupled with her arguably stiff portrayal of Billie Frank allowed many to seize the opportunity to censure the project as a near-fatal failure—misguided, melodramatic, and spectacularly overblown. Indeed, Carey’s sharp commercial recession dovetailed well with America’s acute need for cathartic laughs, and so, the singer would become the comedic distraction from other, critical events at the time. Glitter was released on September 11th, 2001.

Now, nearly a quarter century after the fact, pop gold can be mined from this soundtrack as an artifact of a bygone era. For the artist, for music historians like me, and for fans of pop history, such retrospection towards pop’s flops allows us to examine the lasting ways that works like Glitter make their impact, even if it isn’t at the summit of the Billboard 200. An instant cult classic, now finding its footing as a work of kitsch, its accompanying soundtrack and its four singles represent an adventurous mélange of pop, funk, hip-hop and R&B, fused together with harmonious fun that few other people than Mariah Carey are capable of.

Take the album’s first single. The “Loverboy (Remix) begins with a “pop,” and the track hits with a firecracker spark that explodes into a charged barrage of lusty come-ons between raunchy rappers. Mariah enters the melee, singing in delirious ecstasy over how good her lover makes her feel. The pop song equivalent of the best parts of mania, the “Loverboy (Remix)” crams hypersexuality, patriotic imagery, thinly veiled jabs at Mariah’s rival Jennifer Lopez, drag racing, hub caps, and a cavalcade of rappers in four-and-a-half minutes of nonstop thrill.

Pushing the envelope, “Loverboy” is far beyond the threshold of earlier chart-topping hits in Carey’s catalogue. Much like Lux Lisbon, the amorous anti-hero from Jeffrey Eugenides’ The Virgin Suicides, Carey’s first outing for Virgin was anything but. The demure quality of “Fantasy,” “Honey,” and “Heartbreaker,” were shed on the fun, funky, and suggestive “Loverboy”. Carey’s newfound sexual candor took centerstage as she crooned and frothily cooed about her lover, her sugar daddy, how his lovin’ stoked her insatiability.

Sonically, Carey was committed as ever to the world of the amusement park. High-noted whees recall the titillation of a rapidly descending rollercoaster, and the first staccato “ahh” at the album’s conclusion featuring Cameo are the closest thing to a Mariah Carey Pepsi commercial, if she didn’t make her own six years later. Engineered to be a literal blast from end to end, “Loverboy” resulted from Carey ‘s collaboration with record producer Clark Kent. Their mission? To replace “Loverboy’s” old sample—Yellow Magic Orchestra’s “Firecracker”—with the sound of Cameo’s “Candy”, thus creating a jauntier take on the 1983 song.

Carey’s hazy female lead vocal is introduced by guest rappers Da Brat, Ludacris, 22 and Shawna. Though at the time, many claimed Carey had been drowned out in a crowded song, Carey is participating in a hip-hop precedent which is now normal practice in popular music. I can immediately think of the lengthy list of collaborators on My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy (2010), Beyoncé (2013), and Renaissance (2022) to name a few.

With minimal radio exposure, “Loverboy” holds the dubious honor of breaking Mariah’s #1 streak by peaking at the penultimate on the Hot 100, strategically held from #1 by Destiny’s Child’s “Bootylicious”. Nevertheless, the hit resulted from Virgin Records executives slashing the price of the single by 83% and the widespread frenzy that fomented around speculations of Carey’s illness. Selling the song for 49 cents catapulted the song up 58 positions, a tectonic movement then that’s commonplace on today’s charts. Though Mariah and Virgin were derided for “manipulating” the charts, most songs are sold for the same price today.

Today, artists as sexually permissive as Peaches or Kim Petras make Mariah’s verses seem passé. But in context, the raciness of Mariah’s lyrics, “His loving takes me high/ like a taste of ecstasy/all I need for him is to be my lover boy,” risked leveraging Carey’s maturation to pique curiosity. Despite lukewarm success, “Loverboy” pays cultural dividends. Its salaciousness, never seen by a singer of Carey’s pedigree, was propelled by her erotic singing, giving inspiration and rationale to a cadre of younger female musicians singing authentically about sexuality. Ariana Grande’s ode to the romp in “Side to Side” could not be conceived without “Loverboy.” The song expanded the expressive range for women to include their sexual voracity.

For being at the cutting edge of several breakthroughs in popular music (sonic, strategic, and scintillating), “Loverboy” merits a deserving second listen. It is the harbinger of a paradigm shift in the sale and promotion of popular singles, a foretelling the tale of pop’s further entanglement with hip-hop in the 2000s, and America’s fodder when the country lived through a waking nightmare.

Its muddled release aside, “Loverboy” boasts genius writing, incomparable singing, and lurid imagery. Lambs—the name Carey gave to her fanbase—have more ways to celebrate “Loverboy” today than during its original chart run. Thanks to a lamb-led #justiceforGlitter campaign in 2018, Glitter mounted an impressive comeback. So too should its Hip-Hop/Funk-Pop lead single be revisited for its triumphs.

title: Before the Spotlight Dimmed (Televison Critique)
body:
Before the Spotlight Dimmed:

Dionne Warwick & Burt Bacharach at The Kraft Music Hall (1970)

Television Critique

Most marriages make the mistake in believing it takes two to make a thing go right. But it just so happens that three will give you better chances at success in matrimonial peace and order. Like most business arrangements, marriages fare better when opportunities for two-sided antagonism and opposition are minimized.

Like the holy trinity, triads foment balance and stability, and command respect and reverence. Though I can thank other alliances that flourished in stable longevity, such as Peter, Paul, and Mary or Janet Jackson, Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis, nowhere is this more evident than in the musical marriage between composer Burt Bacharach, songwriter Hal David, and the divine Dionne Warwick.

Within pop music, where musical marriages seem to begin in heaven and quickly end in hellish flames, Bacharach, David, and Warwick prospered for nearly ten solid years—an eternity in the music industry. Between the three of them, an entire era (1962-1971) of successful releases for Scepter Records made for a unique soundtrack—a constant, alternative mélange of sound for the most turbulent decade in twentieth century America.

As a training music historian, I’ve learned how knowing the history and context about the process and creation of pop music can avail me to witness the magic of working relationships, such as the one between Warwick, David and Bacharach. I am left with the license to lose myself in the old magic of an enchanting voice, guided by poignant and fitting lyrics and propelled by pleasantly complex arrangements.

That said, I have minimal interest in serial television and film. I recognize that this retrospective examines a televised special from 1970, a time and sound that should seem foreign to me. (I’m a millennial.) I also recognize I lack the minimum of television acumen. When asked to review television, I became hard pressed to find a show to watch. For someone who devotes all TV time to MSNBC, Judge Judy reruns, and archival footage of female vocalists, however, The Kraft Music Hall program spoke to me early one morning in September. Roused from a deep sleep at 4 AM, I was startled but immediately connected to what I watched: Dionne Warwick singing, “Make It Easy on Yourself.” I took the cue and decided to review the program.

In June 1970, shortly after the release of I’ll Never Fall in Love Again, Warwick appeared with Bacharach on NBC as part of The Kraft Music Hall: An Evening with Burt Bacharach, one of a series of musical variety television specials that appeared on the network between 1958 and 1971. (Named after the sponsor, the Kraft corporation—the one and the same responsible for inedible mac and cheese.) Appearances from French singer and guitarist Sacha Distel and actor Joel Grey were broadcasted alongside Warwick’s segments; these scenes—perhaps scripted—provide us with an intimate look at the moments that reify the relationship Bacharach enjoyed with David and Warwick.

Dressed in a show gown of purple chiffon with a green and pink foliate motif, Warwick beautifully performed, “What the World Needs Now,” a new arrangement of her 1962 demo “Make It Easy on Yourself,” as well as “Loneliness Remembers What Happiness Forgets,” the last of which also featured in a warm recording session between vocalist and her composer. Led by Bacharach on piano, the two reminisced on their years together while performing a medley of earlier hits including “Walk on By,” “Alfie,” and “I’ll Never Fall in Love Again” amongst others.

I admire Warwick’s vocal timing and enjoy her comedic restraint in her subtle retorts to Bachrach’s suggestions about songs, vocal range, and their partnership—funny, but likely toned-down for television. For example, when Bacharach mentioned paying Warwick $15 per demo, she quips, “Nuh-uh. It was twelve dollars and fifty cents.” The laughs continue when she’s asked if she remembers her demo for “Make it Easy on Yourself.” Perhaps to throw minimal shade, Warwick pretends to forget songs she recorded for $12.50. The chemistry full of warm wit, Warwick’s stardom finds parity in partnership with David and Bacharach.

Together, the company of three created a pop holy trinity. The unseen songwriter in David, breathes the words of life into Bacharach’s arrangements, which then find precision and accuracy as they leave Warwick’s lips. Peppered in attractive charisma, Bacharach, the musically omnipotent composer, resembles the reassuring father who encourages his child to sing songs requiring two octaves. And of course, the public-facing counterpart, Warwick basks in the glow of the spotlight. She glorifies, converts, and saves all through the gospel of music. What Bacharach calls her “perfection” is her smart and subtle sense of lilt, which is on full display in the special. For those to care to hear, she shares her divinity to save us all from perdition.

Luck would have it, Bacharach reflects, that working with professionals like Dionne Warwick and Hal David would result in the several hit singles, of which, no such formula existed. And while I agree that the formula did not exist in the individual songs written and performed, the magic in the marriage between the trio is found in their foundation, “built on love and understanding. Her love of music and our understanding of her great talent” induced our enchantment with Warwick’s seeming ease for many years while she sang Bacharach’s complex arrangements and expressed David’s melancholic sentiment.

Yet, as luck would have it, I reflect, this televised special is bittersweet in retrospect. Soon after its airing, the match made in heaven—a critical component of Warwick’s new recording contract with Warner Bros.—would divorce. This time, over the monetary failure caused by the box office bomb, Lost Horizon (1973). Warwick’s career would not recover until her comeback in 1979’s Dionne, but this time, without David and Bacharach. What I witnessed at The Kraft Music Hall occurred before the spotlight dimmed. We were entreated to a final moment in a marriage of sweet musical magic, the likes of which, are a beloved rarity today.

The Queer Aesthetics of Dionne Warwick  - A Fashionable Analysis
body:
The Queer Aesthetics of Dionne Warwick: A Fashionable Analysis

Kwame Kruw Ocran, PhD Candidate, Music, University of Pennsylvania

Pop Con 2025: Baby It’s a Look! Popular Music, Style, and Fashion at the Edge

March 14th, 2025

Veneration

The six-decade long career of Dionne Warwick has been that of the consummate lady—sophisticated, ravishing and witty. At 84, the recording artist and celebrity has mastered the art of making an entrance. Her title, Queen of Twitter, goes uncontested, and while I do venerate her as such, this is probably my best chance to convince her to make the jump to BlueSky.

From her recent appearance at the 2024 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony, it became very clear that she also is the master of how and when to leave the room. With sincere gratitude, she had very little to say: “I’m gonna just say this and get on off the stage: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.”

Thank you, Ms. Warwick, for your inimitable contributions to music. Her welcome to the Hall of Fame recognizes her formidable body of work, a repertoire that rivals that of Aretha Franklin, Diana Ross, and Patti LaBelle.

What sets Warwick apart from the standard guard of black female vocalists in the sixties, seventies, and eighties is her peculiar performativity, her gossamer-like, silken timbre that guaranteed her ability to leverage crossover appeal for many years.

In addition, Warwick, a trained musician, parleyed her abilities to sightread music as well as her formative experiences within the church and as part of the Gospelaires. Together, these experiences allowed the performer to pursue technically demanding arrangements with precision and accuracy. Vocal performances that are ubiquitously Dionne, too many to name but include 1962’s “Don’t Make Me Over,” 1967’s “I Say a Little Prayer” and 1979’s “I’ll Never Love This Way Again”. Dionne’s voice proved immensely popular at a time when American popular music began to understand audience interest and desire.

Late Night Calling

For someone who devotes all his TV time to Judge Judy reruns, and archival footage of Mariah Carey, I was startled by my algorithm one September morning, just after 4 AM, The sound was familiar, unexpected, but at first sight, I was immediately connected: I saw Dionne Warwick singing, “What the World Needs Now.” I took the cue and set out to study the program.

Warwick’s segments singing and in repartee with Bacharach; these scenes—perhaps scripted—provide us with an intimate look at the moments that defined the relationship she enjoyed with Bacharach and David.

At Penn, I’ve studied Dionne Warwick’s career and music under Anthony DeCurtis to consider a method of longform criticism from studying the written record, in part. Contemporary critics argued that Warwick relied on professional relationships with Burt Bacharach, Hal David, Barry Manilow and Clive Davis to continue her recording career and that she lacked very little performative agency herself.

As a black woman whose creative control served as the aural bottleneck from music written by white men, the very foundation of Warwick’s stardom proved problematic for critics charged with making sense of popular music. Feature pieces in her honor, such as Nick Toches’s 1972 profile, wrestled with her genre, “Dionne Warwick isn’t a rock’n’roll singer. She’s not a jazz singer either. Rhythm and blues? Nope. A pop singer? No way.”

Though such accusations could not be farther from the truth, Warwick possesses a performativity that works from beyond an opaque interior. She is vocally arresting, but perhaps guarded, or even performing a public-facing role. While her vocality maintains a subtle defiance resisting genre classification, and her energies as a celebrity are indicative of an alternative modes, I argue that Warwick’s sartorial choices are a yet another transmission of opaque interiority.

My thesis is this: Dionne Warwick effuses an attractive queerness that can be perceived in her vocality and her attire. Warwick’s ability to persist with an air of sophistication in sound and presentation is a testament to her performance of an opaque interiority. Warwick’s queerness resulted in rock criticism that could never arrest her to genre, nor pin her physique outside of slender compliment. I refer to Oxford’s fundamental definitions: strange, odd, peculiar, eccentric, and I desire to investigate the queerness of her style as an overt refusal of sexuality in the promotion and release of her music.

The Dress

Dressed in a show gown of purple chiffon with a green and pink foliate motif, Warwick beautifully performed, “What the World Needs Now,” a new arrangement of her 1962 demo “Make It Easy on Yourself,” as well as “Loneliness Remembers What Happiness Forgets,” the last of which also featured in a warm recording session between vocalist and her composer. Led by Bacharach on piano, the two reminisced on their years together while performing a medley of earlier hits including “Walk on By,” “Alfie,” and “I’ll Never Fall in Love Again” amongst others.

As a fan, I am attracted to Warwick’s lilt—her vocal timing, the swing of her strong belting into the breathless air of her head voice, the voice wrapped within its rasp, her sung and spoken vocalizations. I enjoy her comedic restraint in her subtle retorts to Bachrach’s suggestions about songs, vocal range, and their partnership—they’re pleasantly funny, but likely toned-down for television.

Re-watching Bacharach and Warwick’s chemistry, however, I never thought of thought of her dress. I thought that to be peculiar from what I’ve known about fan worship of female celebrities and musicians, the ensemble always takes part of the equation. What was different about Dionne?

In the same vein, any awareness of Warwick’s off-stage persona had proved elusive for decades, almost as though she could delineate her private affairs from her celebrity. Then again, we have flashes of strangeness that suggest a definite quirk in her off-stage antics.

In the seventies, Warwick spent most of her nearly hit-less period at Warner Brothers with a stylized ‘e’ at the end of her last name, as directed by a numerologist.

Leading the charge in the nineties against misogyny in rap, Warwick directly confronted rapper Snoop Dogg at her home, suggesting he reduce the presence of certain words in his music, and he obliged.

And upon her 2002 arrest for possession of several joints, she disavowed the use of any drug—including aspirin, and we obliged.

Save for these few and far between incidents, Warwick has remained the primary force in her on-stage celebrity and persona while largely keeping mum about her off-stage activities.

This paper celebrates Dionne Warwick’s quirk, her strangeness in her dress, and her queer vocality—the silk-like sound that tells us nearly nothing of its source but allows us to see deeply into ourselves. In her career, Ms. Warwick, so polished and pristine in her fashion, inspires questions about desirability, sexuality, interiority, and music criticism.

Queer Where There Is Love

In a 1973 op-ed on Warwick and her upcoming album Just Being Myself, music critic David Nathan charges Warwick as being a charming young lady, who “totally has feminine air about her”. This comes after reporters cheekily asked her “What makes a female feminine?” An interesting question to pose to Warwick; the brunt of praise she received, none of the other ladies I juxtaposed with Warwick would be affronted with questions about their femininity. Matched by a natural desire to know and to reveal, our intention to implicate someone’s sexuality, Warwick encounters questioning that suggests the presence of a strangeness in her life.

While in Europe, particularly in Paris, Warwick was taken under the wing of Hollywood actress Marlene Dietrich during her first tour. It was Dietrich who proved instrumental in introducing Warwick to European fashion couture, thus contributing a significant change to Dionne’s sartorial sensibilities.

There remains the question given what we know of Dietrich—of her bisexuality and her predilection for the underground bars of Paris and Europe—and of Dionne Warwick—a young Black American ingenue raised within the strict confines of the black church—of whether more can be speculated of their relationship than a simple mentorship and sartorial advice.

Did Dietrich introduce Warwick to the thriving gay bars of Europe? Could they have become lovers? Quite possibly, but given the lack of evidence and Warwick’s desire to guard private matters, this remains a matter of speculation

Dionne, when placed next to others who proved their popular longevity during her major charting years (1962-1992) possesses s a difference in sexuality, interiority, and music criticism. Also, slender and equally beautiful, but far less vocally talented, Diana Ross found herself on equal footing of adulation at the apex of Dionne’s years with Bacharach and David. This meant that as Diana continued to prevail as Motown’s darling, comparisons, competition, and other questions were asked of Dionne. Her documentary Don’t Make Me Over features reporters asking questions about the possibility of her joining Motown’s ranks, to which she fans away the attention with grace.

Warwick’s queerness is more capacious than an investigation into clandestine same-sex relationships, though a longer meditation on her escapades in Europe with Marlene Dietrich in the early sixties could prove illuminating.

Nevertheless, I declare and study Warwick as a site of refusal that is decidedly queer. Her vocality, and the sound she cultivated with Bacharach and David, and later with Manilow and Davis resisted reductive mandates governing the curation, and cultural production of 1960s popular music. She didn’t have to be and chose not to be sexy.

Further, with a sound that garnered cachet in both black and white audiences, Warwick had an appeal and presentation that made it difficult to relegate her to a single genre, rendering her sonically illegible for rock critics. As a result, Warwick was never the critical darling that Diana or Aretha became.

Speaking of Fashion

To speak to Dionne Warwick’s fashionable queerness, I make use of Michael Mohammed’s definition of vocality, where all the singer’s vocal manifestations are “invested with social meaning and not wholly determined by its linguistic content.”

Perhaps, Warwick decided to invest her fashion with social meaning, not wholly determined by its fabric or its hem. What statements do her choices in clothing make after six decades?

What intersectional social meanings are derived by Warwick, an artist who found derision from rock critics? What aspects or elements of Warwick’s vocality, or her fashion proved illegible to us at the time? What aspects of her fashion remain illegible, especially when its social meaning, not the physical construction of her dresses, determine her femininity, celebrity, and even her paradoxical right to privacy?

And why was the need to categorize so important to the examination of Warwick’s tenure as a popular vocalist? And if we continue her life beyond her voice, we may be led to ask ourselves, what queer affirmations from Warwick’s tenure as a celebrity sustain, encourage, and enliven?

If we can accept what signifies Warwick’s distinct voice, the unique sounds it makes, perhaps we can also behold what signifies Warwick’s distinct style, and sartorial choice.

Parallel to her sound, a mélange of pop, jazz, gospel, and rhythm-and-blues, Warwick’s impeccable wardrobe points to a liminality that is at once nondescript and confounding. Often wearing beautiful gowns—a gift from her days in Paris with Dietrich—Warwick received rave reviews from her slender figure but never showed it.

Due to its strange presentation in American popular music—covered on television, a forum that sells and trades in sex—it’s strangely admirable to find a female vocalist who sold so much in that same market without yielding to more amorous standard. In an industry where the insatiable demand for celebrity intimates operates on sexiness as currency, Warwick evaded both “selling out” and participating in a “respectability politics” by not cashing her body in to drive profits towards her musical craft. Perhaps incidental, or maybe a reflection of her values, her choice in fashion matches a lack of intense sexuality in her music.

Though today, we regard Warwick’s sound with a timbre that feels at home with an intersection of blackness and womanhood. Her celebrity and vocality remained unfettered by regimented genre categorization, the clamor for suggestive ensembles, and even sexual classification, too.

The chronology of her public decisions and private matters makes for a celebrity that deserves deeper inquiry. The sound and style of Dionne Warwick leaves an inimitable legacy that render her longstanding career impossible to follow. They also render her very queer.

Discipline: A Study of Cindy Lozito
body:
Discipline: A Study of Cindy Lozito, Artist

(Longer Profile Draft)

I. Sonic Palette

People who call themselves “artists” are spendthrift with their abilities to make others take notice. Look no further than our modern-day Hedda Hopper: rapper Azealia Banks was once considered to be the one to usurp Nicki Minaj with her rapid-fire venom; now, she wastes her special concoction on leveraging small notoriety for her turn at churning the rumor mill. What would become of her if other stories were miraculously clear of guile? What clout can she boast of her career given its severe deflation?

Self-fashioned and consistently productive, there’s an echelon of contemporary creative artists that boast total control over their professional livelihoods—and keep the lights on. Clear as a bell, such voices pierce through the smoke and trickery of the glamoured glitz and reach the ears of an unsuspecting audience with an aligned, authentic vision. Instead of relying on the artifice of a contrived narrative, small truths prevail in the midst of their artistic expression. Often discovered and celebrated, perhaps, sometimes, too quickly, hinders how well we process the greatness of their artistic statement.

There are others, still, who sustain a certain visibility, even in periods of artistic refinement and transformation. Success permits them to indulge in moments of self-reflection. The more some artists strive to become themselves, the more the public clamors for their new works. Yet even in this case, years of work gone unseen, ceaseless toil, and many, many moments of self-doubt are trounced too-soon by fabricated notions of “the overnight sensation.”

Janet Jackson’s breakthrough third album, Control (1986) and her retrospective Design of a Decade, 1986-1996 immediately come to mind. Neither Janet’s acting chops, nor her last name garnered her the platform she eventually found on her own, through her own creation. It was her sonic, visual, and spiritual choices as a creative that made her a darling of the public for several decades and allowed her creative freedom to blossom.

For me, Jackson’s cheery single from Design, “Runaway,” had always intimated itself as the farthest thing from strategic calculation and choreography, even in my childhood. I always understood the song’s feeling to suggest an unplanning of adult monotony, the unraveling of the tight hold we place upon ourselves, and the allowance of the unabashed fun of a whirlwind romance. Of course, productions like “Runaway” require the artist to perform their work—the finely appointed and color coordination of Cindy Lozito’s wedding ceremonies and displays were no exception. The faint baby blue colored accented scarves of silk, the blue and orange self-designed invitation and thank you notes, the curated table arrangements, and that baby blue rotary phone that lives rent-free in my mind, a phone re-engineered to allow guests only to leave the newlyweds a good luck message—each element appeared seamless to me and a clear sign that the affair took as much of Cindy’s time and careful attention like the results of her artistry in Philadelphia. Perhaps like Jackson’s popular single, Cindy’s wedding was one of several highlights that signaled an arrival, a celebration, and a moment of reflection. After all, her journey so far was also ten years in the making.

With Jackson’s “Runaway” and Cindy’s wedding in mind, I thought it indeed right and salutary that I named a previous, admittedly top-heavy profile on Cindy Lozito after Janet’s Design of a Decade (1995). Knowing Cindy for a decade and a half, and in speaking in light of the overnight narrative, I dedicated the adventure of profiling her to tell her origin story: the Latina kid from Queens and Christ the King High School who heeded tremendous lessons while gaining informative experience in her journey to life as an artist in Philadelphia. “Cindy Lozito, Design of a Decade 2014-2024”, though well-intentioned, was notably incomplete. This second piece, named “Cindy Lozito: Discipline,” pays proper attention to the development of Cindy’s artistry, her tenacity in her ability to marshal all she is into the creation of vivid, imaginative, inviting pieces, and an invitation posed by the foundation of her art. Knowing Cindy and what she’s experienced, her work carries deeper meaning for me because I see her work inspired by her life, whether it’s a comic, a display, or a large mural. It became very important to me, with Design, to detail her narrative of challenge, struggle, and grit.

In searching for inspiration for “Discipline” as a deeper look into Cindy’s artwork, artistic practices, and beliefs, I returned to our hours long interview in October at my studio apartment. During the last hour of footage, Cindy curated a Spotify Playlist with me. Strangely enough, shortly after our interview, I shuffled the track listing and added four songs I thought Cindy would approve of, fattening the playlist time to a healthy hour and a half, to then be recorded onto a faulty, 90-minute Maxell XLII cassette that I intended to give her for her birthday (Only the real ones know). Instead, it sat next to my stereo for weeks. I played the warped tape to revisit Cindy’s sonic palette for this piece, and the musical tea leaves made so much sense.

The cassette played its first tracks: “Welcome to My Island” by Caroline Polachek, “Sympathy is a Knife” by Charli XCX, and Chappell Roan’s “Pink Pony Club.” I became astonished. These musical signposts, along with Janet’s Design, were absolutely no fluke. Like Cindy, these artists also endeavored through periods of longsuffering and toil. When acclaim came, these artists were improperly exposed to the notion of overnight discovery, immediate sensation, and fame. Not only did Cindy choose songs that she enjoyed this season, but she also chose artists that intimately understood the experience of working without recognition for a time, only to confront a sudden onslaught of praise.

Of course, none of the artists mentioned here, save for maybe Ms. Banks, would ever cite ingratitude for praise. But my sense about artists of Cindy’s caliber is that they are due the welcome of a hero’s return from an odyssey of self-discovery and self-possession, two integral ingredients that directly decides how their art connects. However, that’s not our media.

Several songs Cindy selected represented her youth, such as the chorded enchantment of Alicia Keys’ “You Don’t Know My Name,” and her time in college: Marina’s “Starring Role” stood out as a shared staple from playlists in undergrad: back when Cindy took Art History seriously, when I grappled with Political Philosophy, and Marina counted us both as two of her many diamonds. The friend who welcomed me to Philly by furnishing a circular rug upon which my feet rest at the current moment, I count Cindy as one of my musical tastemakers (but she doesn’t know that). She made sure to include the wayfaring, wistful “Voyager” from Birdy’s Young Heart album, an ode to falling leaves and guitar-led separation. Their themes of womanhood and agency create a sonic image of her personality and taste; she is the one leads the creation of sentimental possibilities, the one who refuses to merely support, and the one who prefers to traverse the world unfettered. These come time mind as I render an image of Cindy’s from her choices in popular music.

By asking her to select her favorites in October, I’d venture that engaging with Cindy this way at that moment was well-timed; it finds her brimming with future possibility while reaffirming a faithful statement to herself: to continue to be unsurprisingly vivid, funky, and cool. Curated by the ear of an artist with an eye for poignant sentimentality, Cindy’s mixtape reflects who she is at her core: an eclectic capable of stoking the imagination’s desires for connection, family and community. This investigation into her sonic, visual, and spiritual palettes, her sense of creation, and her process warmly invites new audiences to think of how art lends itself as to the care of communities but intently challenges the idea of Cindy’s artistic success as “overnight.” Following the narrative I detailed in “Design of a Decade 2014-2024,” I find Cindy Lozito, muralist, public artist, and designer, ready to be continued to be seen, ready to be continued to be heard, and always prepared to have it all.

II. Visual Palette

Popular culture has reached a point of saturation where the very mention of an “era” seldom goes far without invoking the name “Taylor Swift” and her famed tour. Now that that’s accomplished, it is useful to think of Cindy Lozito’s recent achievements, milestones, and artistic hallmarks as also belonging to a thematic era, whose name is as important as what it represents. For now, I nominate Janet Jackson’s Discipline (2008) as a work that can emphasize Cindy’s current effort and artistry. A deliberate name, prevailing idea, and concept, Discipline possesses the cache and definition needed to bound the artist’s thoughts and deeds within her current era, when early sketches evolved and appeared as part of a completed piece and changed even further in promotion and advertisement. Organized yet fun, the artist keeps keen focus on locating cohesive elements among several works completed within the same season—all capable of standing alone. When taken together this season, however, her offerings make a formative statement on temporality, resilience, and community.

As part of her practice, Cindy venerates the recurrence of symbolic meaning in her work, such as the presence of the butterfly:

When I'm creating murals for a community or organization, I like to think of my work as either representing or inspiring imagination within that group. Butterflies have shown up a lot in my work during this season in my career, and I've used them as symbols of hope, wonder, and temporality.

Elegantly, Cindy evokes the strength of a butterfly as a defining inspiration during her Discipline era. Her rendering refashions how the popular trope is seen; where convention usually associates the butterfly with narratives of transformation and freedom, Cindy meditates instead on feeling the hope that freedom inspires, spurred by a wonder of the unknown, especially the experience of internal growth. Given Cindy’s own experiences of hope, exploration, and constant change, she needs no rationale for citing the butterfly so meaningfully.

Butterflies abound in Cindy’s works but is celebrated in three distinct appearances this era. The first, an homage to the monarch butterfly, is an orange light box adorned with several flittering monarchs, the largest of which carries the message, “Cuando trabajas a tus sueňos, se convierte en realidad”—roughly meaning, “When you work on your dreams, they come true.” The work is more than a beacon of warm, orange light: it tells an integral part of the origin story of Mexibike, the bicycle shop in South Philadelphia and its owner, Maria, a woman who emigrated with her family from Puebla, Mexico. Maria expressed her hardships and difficulties to Cindy in interviews but persisted in hope. Cindy later recalled, “[Maria] sees the shop as an avenue for hope and prosperity for her children as they grow.”

Offset by black, browns, and shades of yellow, the striking light box is pleasantly reminiscent of drinking Tang at home after school and shows a clear throughline from Maria’s life experience to showcasing her determination to overcome hardship. By featuring Maria’s serious hope wrapped in the ruse of large, expansive, free butterfly wings, Cindy’s creation lingered in my mind as the light box’s arresting glow proved itself worthy of my lengthening gaze.

A large blue and indigo butterfly with anthropomorphic eyes piques child-like curiosity in “Between the Trees,” a mural commissioned this year for the (PMA) of Art’s group show, “Metamorphosis: Celebrating Creativity and Growth” (2024). Inspired by the feeling brought on by the dawn of Spring, Cindy explains that the butterfly represents “the way we all become attuned to colors and shapes in our environment when winter finally shakes away.” Featuring the butterfly as a leader to others, Cindy captures how nature commands us to behold, its beauty and mystery, specifically in the wondering mind of a child. Not only does the butterfly promote a calming effect in “Between the Trees,” Cindy’s character selection beautifully sings the song of diversity. As someone with curly hair, I feel very seen by Cindy’s hair-painting techniques, and am called to pay greater attention to nature’s mystery.

The last invocation of the butterfly arrived as part of the PMA’s Hispanic & Latinx Heritage month exhibition. Cindy’s arresting contribution, The Fabric of Belonging (pictured left), employs harmonious greens and oranges to create an exquisite bandana with corners of coqui tree frogs and small but mighty resting, orange butterflies. In the accompanying giveaway piece (below), Cindy features several topaz and aquamarine butterflies as “guardians resting on the border of a fabric-shaped collage showing photos of my Puerto Rican family members, many of whom have passed away and whom I honored through the piece.” As an exploration of Puerto Rican identity through kitsch, symbolism, and bright colors, Cindy’s collaboration with PMA honored her grandmother’s work as a seamstress, incorporated family photos and showcased colloquial staples of Latinidad, such as the Boricua necklace, Agua de Florida (Florida Water) and Vick’s Vapor Rub.

I get the impression that these three glimpses into Cindy Lozito’s artistry suggest much more than a predilection to butterfly imagery or the tendency to incorporate variations on orange (which also happens to pop on Cindy’s website, cindylozito.com). The butterflies summoned for the Mexibike light box, “Between the Trees” and The Fabric of Belonging reinforce the expression and presence of Cindy’s interiority as a Latinx woman, a talented artist, a kind altruist and an ambitious creator intent on becoming herself through the creation of her art. Self-expression and self-possession; given Cindy’s journey, this should never be taken for granted.

III. Spiritual Palette

I return to calling these this era Cindy’s Discipline as a useful way to preserve the highlights of Cindy’s season, to (un)officially recognize the start, the end, as well as the distinct flavor of the creative energies that made her success possible. Like Janet in 2008, Cindy in 2024 continued to pay homage to her identity and style even when it may not have been in vogue. The crisp, funky, and deceptively light production on Discipline (2008) created a vibe that invited diverse audiences to feel and to move. Cindy’s artistry—elevated further by her idiosyncratic style—makes audiences feel and fawn as well. Her kinships with butterflies, the visual palette of orange—a color that emblemizes optimism, happiness, creativity, warmth, energy, enthusiasm, as well as success, willpower, independence, achievement, determination, freedom, and health—contains the same power that Janet yields in her iconic choreography: both artists strive continually to recognize their artistic genius.

Always armed with dedication and tenacity, Cindy Lozito now boasts a robust portfolio that can certainly speak for itself. From her days in her freelancer-corporate era (c. 2017) Cindy’s work at Health Union flourished; during that time, she created five to nine illustrations weekly, refining the talents and skills she amassed from her earlier days as part of Art Girl Army, a post-college creative salon. She leveraged her skills to illustrate multiple articles for The Washington Post, the New York Times, the LA Times, and completed her first murals at the Philadelphia Flower Show (2022) and close by her South Philadelphia home in 2023. Sharing the mural making process in the name of reciprocity, Cindy allowed the community to join the creation process of “Seasons of Reciprocity,” a commission for Metropolitan Hospital’s “Arts in Medicine Campaign” in New York. Scenes from the event saw Cindy marshaling music, donorship, public and private entities under the auspices of her art. A decade in the making, Cindy’s artistry continues to astonish Philadelphia’s art world with humility and aplomb.

There isn’t a winning formula to success as an artist today. However, I am sure the secret to Cindy’s success lies in her mastery of the carefully coiffed seemingly effortless promotional campaign—the very stuff of an upcoming or a celebrated era. To properly entice audiences and patrons alike via an advertising blitzkrieg, the artist must commit to setting and meeting deadlines, promoting themselves, establishing and maintaining connections, appearing in public, performing with hopes to channel the zeitgeist, engaging with the press; it is, of course, work!

Unlike many artists and celebrities who possess a slimy film of narcissism in their engagement with us common folk, Cindy relies upon a bedrock raison d’etre that needs others (her audience, her patrons, her students) to articulate her vision and keep her grounded. In between seeing Wicked, concluding her season, and the commencement of the holidays, she shared the following:

If someone recognizes themselves through my art in a flower that grew in their home country or a motif that reminded them of something from childhood, it feels like forging a bridge of belonging for us both. Whether I'm creating art for murals, online illustrations, books, or other outlets somewhere down the line, I hope to always foster this type of connection through my work.

Cindy’s tender commitment to forging bridges of belonging is central to who she is as an artist and individual. In making others feel seen, in allowing for audience reciprocity, and in following the yearn of her internal transience, she keeps humble and eager without compromising her leadership and creativity or using her talents for selfish reasons. (We’re looking at you, Azealia.)

With a sonic palette that aligns with catharsis and taste, and a visual palette that is a conduit for healing and community, Cindy lives a life that is spiritually aligned with her intentions. Further supported by doting husband Nick and the cutest dog ever, Percy, Cindy lives her truth successfully as an artist and a creative, something that not everyone has.

Though misguided, the recent clamor for Cindy this season is well-deserved, as she is someone whose already lived through several eras, who invested herself into becoming a productive powerhouse with an uncanny panache for organization. While it is glamorous witnessing a beautiful unfolding in Cindy’s positive reception this year, it would be remiss of me not to pay attention to detail of her origin story and the evolution of her art. After all, she is an artist who in articulating her vision, consults each stakeholder as they pour their perspective into her mixture, from which she brews universal themes in spectacular hues.

For my song response, I decided to analyze “Ball & Chain” by Big Mama Thornton because I really enjoy expressive guitar work and felt it was an interesting combination of classic blues with some rock influence. I am a big fan of indie and classic rock and also have a background in Jazz, and I could hear themes of all three in this performance.

Thornton’s vocal timbre is definitely my favorite part of the song, as she displays a rich tonal variety, with a number of powerful growls and rasps, making the delivery especially expressive. She exudes strength, and I’m incredibly impressed and moved by the vulnerability required to perform a song about the heavy burden of loving someone who mistreats you. Such a message was uncommon at a time when songwriters tended to write about more frivolous subjects suited to the conventional male gaze. This context makes Thornton’s performance even more powerful and uniquely vulnerable.

Musically, the slow, easy tempo and swing rhythm contribute to the feeling of being “weighed down,” like the “ball & chain” weighing her down in the lyrics. The song also features simple instrumentation, allowing her voice to take center stage, ultimately giving the performance a much more personal feel. Her voice and the guitar feed off each other in a call-and-response pattern, typical of the blues, making the song feel more conversational, more personal, and, for that, more vulnerable. The pauses between lines are also particularly expressive and heart-wrenching as they convey a sense of struggle in delivering the lyrics, emphasizing the weight of the themes in the song.

While I also liked Janice Joplin’s version, I found her interpretation to be sharper and angrier, with heavy, loud guitar, and piercing screams. Conversely, Big Mama Thornton’s performance conveys both strength and sorrow, making it more personal and, in my opinion, powerful.

I think this song is best listened to, as Mama Thornton puts it: “Sittin’ by my window… lookin’ out at the rain.” It’s a song that requires introspection and reminds us of the importance and strength required to be vulnerable. It also sends a powerful message about the difficulty, but also the necessity, of walking away from those who mistreat you.

This is the version I listened to— definitely worth a listen!

I chose to write about “Sweet Home Chicago” by Robert Johnson, recorded in 1936. I initially chose this song from the playlist for a personal reason, which is that I love listening to songs that reference cities and real-life places. From acoustic pop hits like “Manhattan” by Sara Bareilles (2012) to TV show theme songs like “California (The O.C.)” by Phantom Planet (2006), these types of location-based songs help connect for me what otherwise might feel more like a third party's personal story to more tangible physical spaces that I can visualize. A few years ago, I actually made a playlist of city-based songs for fun.

However, unlike the aforementioned examples, the lyrics of “Sweet Home Chicago” do not serve to describe the titular location of this song. In fact, the lyrical voice/narrator seems to singing from elsewhere in the country, begging his “baby” (0:04) to join him in leaving for Chicago, “the land of California” (0:25), and “Des Moines, Iowa” (2:30). In the context of the Great Migration (Brice), which was still ongoing at the time of this song, one could believe that this is in reference to the movement of Black people in the late 19th and early 20th centuries out of the Jim Crow South and into other regions of the country. Upon further research, some argue that he actually may be singing about the industrial town of Port Chicago in northern California (McClelland). Nonetheless, the idealization of such places far away from the south affirms the inherent Blackness of the narrator's experience, which in turn, adds to the bluesy feeling of both this song and musical genre. This interpretation of the lyrics makes even more sense considering that the Mississippi-born Johnson spent his recording career exclusively in the south (Britannica).

Port Chicago is also situated about an hour from my hometown in the Oakland area, which adds to my personal enjoyment of this particular song – as I only know of Port Chicago from the “Port Chicago Highway” that I’ve driven on a few times, I had no idea that a town used to exist there until this song inspired me to do some additional digging (McClelland). While these potential references to Port Chicago are by no means a musical element by themselves, they add to the historical retrospective that this song naturally creates when listened to in 2024. This song's place is no longer in popular music, but as an artifact of a past American perspective.

Many quintessential elements typical in blues songs appear throughout this track. Johnson’s voice is flexible in both pitch and rhythm, with no vocal harmony to support him. One hears mainly Johnson’s chest voice (e.g. at 2:12), as he sings in a forte volume in many parts of this song. I like that the “shouting” timbre and flexibility of his vocals create a casual, imprecise tone — a conversational feeling that also speaks to the blues’ roots in fieldwork songs sung outdoors. Even when the same lyrics are sung multiple times, the small sonic alterations that Johnson makes allow the song to not feel overly repetitive (e.g. the singing of “To my sweet home Chicago” at 1:24 is much more legato, with the syllables connected and held for a longer duration compared to its prior appearance at 0:58). Upon repeated listens, I notice more small syncopations (0:23) and irregular singing patterns (1:04), which together create the swing rhythm that keeps the song feeling alive and interesting throughout (at least for me).

The melody of the chorus also starts at a high pitch (e.g. “Baby, don’t you want to go?”), then ends much lower to give a sense of melodic closure (“Chicago”). Furthermore, the chorus follows, more or less, the AAB structure commonplace in this genre, with the refrain “Back to the land of California / To my sweet home Chicago” (0:54) serving as a very catchy “B” phrase — as this song has progressively become stuck in my head, it is principally this phrase that I have heard on repeat.

The production of this song — simple vocals atop acoustic strumming — speak to both the song’s place of origin in the south and time period of the 1930s, given that the electric blues began slightly later around the 1940s and more as a result of blues regionalisms (e.g. the Chicago blues). This track serves as a great example many elements of what one could consider to be an older, deeply southern blues song and a narrative of Black self-invention. While I do not foresee it topping my Spotify Wrapped anytime soon, I enjoyed it for its encapsulation of history — reading about its possible subjects and references to the Great Migration made this a fun assignment for me.

I chose to review the song “Waiting for a Train” by Jimmie Rodgers, who sang in his signature “blue yodel” and is sometimes known as the “Father of Country Music”. I watched a performance of this song from the 1929 short film “The Singing Brakeman”, where Jimmie Rodgers sits in front of a railroad station building and performs three songs.

“Waiting for a Train” is performed on a single guitar and vocals, and recounts the story of a penniless man trying to return back home but instead getting kicked off the train. This type of “hillbilly music” targeted the poor, white, adult working class and often had themes of hardship and suffering. The song follows a basic 12-bar blues structure and the instrumental part is not very complex, allowing others to easily sing along. It tells the daily struggles of a poor man trying to find work, which would have been especially relatable for many people during the Great Depression in the 1930s. The tempo is set almost at a speaking speed, giving the sense that Rodgers is languidly telling us his story. Two women are also in the scene, one drying dishes and one sewing an article of clothing, further giving the performance an impression of candidness. Rodgers starts off with a simple guitar intro and then imitates a train whistle, using his mouth to create a cool vocal sound effect (0:11). After the intro, he sings the first verse (0:27), yodels (1:10), sings the second verse (1:19), then yodels again to end the song (2:00). His signature blue yodel feels slower than the rest of the song despite being at the same tempo because the yodeling does not fill the entire space. There are short periods of vocal silence while the guitar strums rhythmically, giving the listener a calm rest before the next verse.

I actually discovered this song on Youtube back when I was in elementary school. I initially liked this song a lot because the tune was catchy yet melancholy, and the lyrics were sad. It was also not too musically-complex for a regular person to sing. As a kid, I would sing this song whenever I was homesick. After listening to it again now, I still like the song, and I appreciate the simplicity of the performance. It’s clearly performative, but it also just feels like a guy singing with a guitar.

“Over The Rainbow,” performed by Judy Garland, was released in 1939 during the Tin Pan Alley music era. Because it was featured in The Wizard of Oz, a prominent American film, the song has reached a broad audience that spans generations and remains popular today. The lyrics describe a heaven-like place where “the dreams that you dare to dream really do come true” (1:06) and where “troubles melt like lemon drops” (1:29). When Garland sings, “that’s where you’ll find me” (1:34), she implies this place is not an unattainable utopia, but a hope for the future. Thus, this song is likely an attempt to help the listener imagine a positive future, specifically during times of personal or widespread hardship. Garland’s emotional performance reinforces this idea as her voice sounds like she is longing to escape her current life to go to the place she is singing about. This theme is particularly significant given that the song was released towards the end of the Great Depression.

Like many songs written during the Tin Pan Alley era, “Over The Rainbow” follows AABA musical form. Although the three A sections (0:31, 0:53, 1:43) have different lyrics after the words “somewhere over the rainbow,” they share the same melody. The B section, which begins with “someday I’ll wish upon a star” (1:15), has a different melody than the A sections and includes a predominantly faster tempo. The melodies in the song are mostly disjunct because they are hard to sing and use many skips and leaps (wide intervals between adjacent notes). In addition, the song has a homophonic texture since it features a prominent melody—sung by Garland—and a less complex accompaniment—played by various instruments.

While this song no longer aligns with my music preferences because it is slow and not energetic, I used to love it when I was younger. As a little girl, I admired Judy Garland’s character in The Wizard of Oz, so I sang “Over the Rainbow” whenever possible. I remember selecting it as my voice recital song in elementary school and singing it with my best friend during a karaoke birthday party. Now, I appreciate Garland’s ability to beautifully sing the jumpy melody and the hopeful theme of the lyrics. Sadly, I can imagine this song being played at a funeral, particularly for people who believe in an afterlife and that death is a passage to a better place.

Muddy Waters’ performance of “I’m Your Hoochie Coochie Man” in 1954 is one of many that solidifies him as the “Father of Chicago Blues.” Composed and written by Willie Dixon to match Waters’ persona as an artist, the piece boasts a sense of narcissism and sexual appeal within the lyrics, heightened by African-American spiritualism. Lines like “ You were born for good luck,” (3:12) and “he gonna make pretty women's, jump and shout” (0:18) all contribute to this idea that he was destined for greatness when it came to attracting women. This fortune Waters sings of stems from “Hoodoo,” spiritual practices and traditions originating among the enslaved in the South and referenced at the start of the second verse: “I got a black cat bone, I got a mojo too

” (0:57).

To complement the spirituality hidden behind Waters’ radiating confidence, the composition follows a steady, adagio tempo, performed at around 75pm in a compound quadruple meter. While Dixon still abides by the standard form of the Blues using the tonic, sub-dominant, and dominant 7th chords, this song follows a 16-bar progression with 4 extra bars of the chord in the song’s key, A major. As to not feel too repetitive however, the harmonica, bass, piano, guitar, and drums all play a conjunct, syncopated riff, first heard at the beginning of the track and throughout the three verses to serve as the “response” to Waters’ “call.” Furthermore, the song's performance style is both instrumentally and vocally expressive. The improvisation of the guitar (1:48) is more disjunct and adds to the strings’ unique timbre, while Waters’ transitions between speaking normally “(1:06) and his emotionally belting (1:27) emphasize both the alluring and spiritual nature of the song.

While the song isn’t one I’d listen to daily, I’ve still come to appreciate the sheer talent showcased with something new after every listen. As someone who’s played a Blues chord progression on the piano in the past, I’ve grown especially fond of the “response” riff and the cadence played descendingly at every turnaround (3:47). Moreover, in the rap scene today with incessant sampling and it’s popular themes of self-esteem and hypersexuality, I can easily see Waters’ recording of lyrics like “I’m him” and“Coochie man” on the next BossMan Dlow, Rob49, or GloRilla track trending on Tik Tok.

I chose to review “A Most Unusual Day” by Beverly Kenney for my musical reflection. To begin, let’s delve into the historical context of the piece. Written in the Tin Pan Alley (TPA) era, this jazz song utilizes the AABA song form with a walking baseline that propels melodic movement. While Beverly’s rendition is from the Jazz era in the 1950s, the song was written during the Tin Pan Alley era. The song alludes to the day being unusual, emphasizing elements of sunshine, human connection, and love blossoming in the vocalist’s day to day life. This alludes to the vocalist being in love, and how this sensation deviates from her norm. Not only is this lyrically expressed, but it is also embedded within the arrangement itself. The deviant vocal melody line and musical jumps in the baseline that so clearly convey standard jazz music elements stray greatly from the norm of Tin Pan Alley ballads, where they are usually slower and have more of an emphasis on the main vocalist. Beverly Kenney sings with a very light, crooning style, which conveys a feeling, to me, of beauty in small moments. At Penn, I am the music director for Counterparts, a group that specializes in pop and jazz a cappella, and whenever we sing jazz music in this style, we target a vibe of carefree vocalizing that purely conveys emotions of bliss. Beverly Kenney has done just that in her recording of “A Most Unusual Day” and the vocal slides and slight vibrato she adds at the end of her sustained notes further contributes towards this overall energy in the song.

Delving further into the musical elements, the polyphony within the arrangement attracts listener attention to each song element, rather than just the vocal melody, which adds depth to the arrangement and message of the song. The first two stanzas are quite predictable in terms of chord structure, which juxtaposes the message of the day being unusual, however in the B section the chord structure and melody deviates before returning to the predictable A section. After the third A section, there is another B followed by more A sections and a short instrumental section at the end of the piece. There are also slight moments within the piece that stray from the original A melody line, specifically from 0:44-0:51 when Kenney sings the minor third above the regular melody for “it’s a most unusual time”. This strays from what the ear expects, and when Kenney does it again at around 1:12 until 1:17, it is more easily anticipated because the listener has already heard the deviation. This element, in my mind, serves as a metaphor on how musicians during this period began to deviate in their creative processes from the societal standards at the time, both artistically and culturally.

Moving into my emotional reaction individual preferences, this song reminds me of a fresh, spring day and the new beginnings that come with it. When overlaying my own emotions with those of the vocalist, there is a clear parallel between the feelings of love that Kenney is feeling and the rebirth of love and appreciation for beautiful weather that I feel in the springtime. This song also reminds me to let myself relax and experience the sensation of being carefree. So often at Penn, I worry about the pressures of academic deadlines and responsibilities, and this song brings light and refreshing energy into my life. This song also aligns with my preferences for jazz. I’ve been performing at Birdland Jazz Club in New York since I was twelve, and this style of music always brings me back to the special memories I have there. This song is a staple on my holiday playlist, as well as on my springtime playlist. While I recognize that many people today tend to select more contemporary songs for such playlists, I believe this song should continue to be played in various jazz clubs and environments across the country and the world in the 2020s. Its classic jazz form and chord structure is nostalgia-inducing, and the message is still quite relevant today.

Oct 2, 2024 8:09pm| Last reply Oct 4, 2024 12:09am

For this Song review, I chose to review “Lean on Me” by Bill Withers. Released in 1972 as the lead single from his upcoming album, Still Bill, Withers used the song in order to reminisce and offer appreciation for his upbringing in the rural south and show praise for the community and strength he’d witnessed there. At the same time, Withers had just moved to Los Angeles, indicating his own struggle to find place and comfort in his environment. Beyond his own narrative, the song’s story also reflects the tensions and struggles in the United States at the time (Mahncke, 2023). The Civil Rights Movement - famously the campaign to abolish legalized “racial segregation, discrimination, and disenfranchisement” in the US - had officially ended in 1968 (Library of Congress, 2024). Thus, “Lean on Me” offered hope and support for the country at a time of heightened inequality, turmoil, and tension

The lyrics of the song demonstrate the vitality of unity and support for one another. In the chorus, Withers sings “Lean on me, when you’re not strong/And I’ll be your friend/… For it won’t be long/Till I’m gonna need somebody to lean on” (0:52-1:18). The message of the song is clearly one of support for others and to do unto others as you’d have them do unto you. Essentially, Withers is echoing the need to be there for and care for your neighbors as in times of struggle and tension such as in the US at the time, there is an amplified need for unity.

Beyond just the lyrics, Withers delivers his story through the instrumentation and vocal delivery just as effectively. From the opening of the song, Withers’ voice is sincere and calming, almost as though he is reassuring the listeners that things will turn out alright. With the use of a repeating chord progression in C, F, G, C with a response of accent notes, Withers offers an intentionally simple, familiar, and warm instrumentation coupled with heartfulness and fullness in his vocal timbre to set a tone of openness and kindness in the song. As the song progresses, there are instruments added which amplify the message that Withers is sharing about community. For instance, the gospel components of a chorus being added act almost as a metaphor for the community and support Withers is calling for, something that I believe was an intentional choice. It seems as though the implementation of the chorus at 2:05, in the middle of the song, acts as a triumph, an assurance that community will be there and come about when you need them most.

Having attended a Catholic school from Kindergarten through 8th grade, I had to sing this song alongside my classmates for our 3rd grade Christmas show. I remember being so touched by the lyrics and finding them to be empowering when singing them with my friends of 5 years or more at that point. I think it is very communal and important to hear and it brings me joy to have been exposed to it so long ago.

While all of the "A" sections have different lyrics, what ties them together is the shared melody. harmony, and vocal rhythm; on the other hand, the "B" section is a noticeable departure from the repetition of the "somewhere over the rainbow" melody and presents a new sound in the song. The texture of the song is homophonic, meaning that the harmony (the accompaniment) and the melody (Judy Garland) are moving together at the same pace.

Judy Garland's rendition of the song depicts the wistful energy of the lyrics and has a very distinct tone that is characteristic of the time period and its technologies. In terms of instrumentation, the accompaniment is primarily composed of strings and woodwinds, with a little percussion as well. The strings and woodwinds (primarily the oboe and flute) make up the bulk of the intro but largely provide a more homophonic role once the melody begins. The harp provides the most texture once the melody begins, playing a series of arpeggios that evoke the wistful energy of the lyrics.

Withers’ timbre begins rich and mellow, as he tells a story in the first verse, “sometimes in our lives / we all have pain / we all have sorrow / but if we are wise / we know that there’s always tomorrow”. The second verse omits the soulful piano chords and relies on percussion to drive Withers’ message. Withers is joined by a chorus at 2:03, metaphorically signifying the importance of community, something Withers lacked at the time this song was written. The second chorus is accompanied by strings, adding gospel elements to the piece. At 2:58, piano chords return, paying homage to the first verse. Here, Withers sings the same melody as the beginning of the piece, but with a brighter and prouder tone, signifying his triumph over hardship. Jump blues were a popular music style during the 1940s. This style is characterized by relaxed and tuneful swing saxophone solos, simple swing riffs, and lyrics about African American life. Jordan emphasizes his appreciation of the name through repetitive uses of the name “Caldonia.” For a song that is two and a half minutes long, the lyrics are remarkably short, which is typical of the jazzy-blues style which likes to emphasize the instrumentals. The first time we hear Jordan is not until 0:53, one-third of the way through the song. Jordan utilizes different vocal styles throughout the piece; not only does he sing, but he yells “Caldonia,” with an emphasis on the last syllable, and he also uses a talking-like style when discussing his mother in the second verse, starting at 1:40.

The song’s instrumentation is very reminiscent of jazz, with a double bass playing the bass line and an alto saxophone on top adding color, with a trumpet or English horn coming later on the song to add a different tone. There is also a drum and piano that provide rhythm and support. The double bass plays a scale of some sort — distinct from the melody and other instruments, the double bass continuously ascends and descend the scale throughout the song. True to the jump blues genre, the song features a relaxed and swingy saxophone solo at 1:25 and consistent riffs from the bass. The singer uses the swing style and certain vocal techniques to perform the piece in a laid-back, relaxed fashion.

Joan Baez’s 1963 performance of “We Shall Overcome” remains a staple of the Civil Rights Movement, redefining the standards for an effective political tool and certifying itself as the anthem of the largest social movement of the 20th century. In this review, I will dissect the historical context surrounding the song’s composition, then analyze the technicalities of its composition, performance, and lyricism, and finally reflect on the piece from a contemporary perspective.

Although its origins remain unknown, the anthem is believed to be derived from Charles Tindley’s 1901 hymn “I’ll Overcome Someday.” Like the popular adaptation, the original incites encouragement for prevailing through troubling times. Tindley’s work especially resonated with those freed from slavery. The hymn, with lyrics like, “If in my heart I do not yield, I'll overcome someday,” would be nostalgic for those who did in fact overcome enslavement and sang similar negro spirituals to endure the tribulations of captivity. In 1947, the modern adaptation was released in the now-discontinued People’s Songs Bulletin by Zilphia Horton, following a strike against the American Tobacco Company where the hymn was consistently used. The song gained national attention during the Civil Rights Movement, when Pete Seeger, the director of People’s Songs, taught it to activists as it spread like wildfire. Yet, it wasn’t until August 1963, unironically following a tumultuous year including MLK Jr.’s arrest, when the song would reach its acme.

Joan Baez’s performance at the March on Washington added to an already pivotal point in history. She sings at a calm, mezzo-piano volume that’s still heard by the thousands in attendance. Baez’s voice, along with the 250,000 harmoniously singing along and the homophonic strumming of the guitar at a steady rhythm, are the only performing forces. The guitar does a perfect job of contributing to that simple, yet powerful sense of hope. Adding to the simplicity is the primarily conjunct melody, repeated twice against its strophic form in the consonant and easily singable key of G major at an andante tempo. Moreover, the repetition of lines like “we are not afraid” (0:03) three times in the stanza of the first verse, and announced by Baez before the second verse (0:44) are intentional. They reassure listeners and tell them to be brave amid the horrors witnessed by the racial injustices of segregation and Jim Crow. In later recordings with more verses, including Baez’s 1971 rendition of another live performance for her album Carry it On, these affirmations of sorts include “we shall be alright” (1:11) and “we shall live in peace” (1:55), exhibiting similar themes of hope for better times. Baez also uses more artistic expression in the album version with adlibs (2:48) and belting higher notes (2:58), adding to the passion with a more personal feel.

While I didn’t understand the significance and passion that came with the song until after the first listen, I knew I wouldn’t enjoy the song playing it on piano, simply for the sentiment-inducing but dull repetition. Still, I felt nostalgic listening to Baez’s voice as I was reminded of church when everyone would rise at the end of the service singing from hymn books in unison. I also thought about modern political tools like Kendrick Lamar’s “Alright” with the similarly repeated lyric “we gon' be alright,” playing a comparable role in the Black Lives Matter movement as inspiration from its predecessor. Furthermore, in light of the election, I wonder how those unhappy with the results and unsure about the future can use “We Shall Overcome” to help look toward a brighter tomorrow.
